title: Stop, Think, Then Choose
keyIdea: When you face a choice, stop before you act on your first idea. Think of more than one option, and think about what might happen with each one: now and later, for you and for other people. Then choose, and be able to say why. If your choice does not work, go back and try another option.
familyTip: When a small problem comes up at home, like two people wanting the same thing, say the steps out loud together: Stop. What are our options? What might happen with each one? Then choose, and later ask: did it work?

visual.caption: First idea or thought-through choice? Drag each card, or tap it and then tap a box.

items: Count to five, then say how I feel
Ask what else I could do

lab.caption: Flagship lab: stop a first idea, find more options, match options to consequences, compare now and later, choose with a reason.

kid: When something goes wrong, a first idea pops up fast. Often it is to shout, grab or hit back. Stop! Take a breath before you do anything. Stopping gives you time to think.
Next, think of your options. An option is one thing you could do. There is nearly always more than one: say how you feel, fix it together, or ask a grown-up for help.
Then think about what might happen with each option. That is its consequence. Think about now and later, and about you and other people. A choice can feel great now and bad tomorrow.
Now choose, and know why. A good reason says what will happen: I will do my homework first, so it gets done and I still get to play. If your choice does not work, go back and try your next option.
adult: Ages 7 to 9. This matches responsible decision-making in the CASEL framework: name the problem, think of ways to solve it, and weigh what is likely to happen for you and for others. It also matches the IB PYP personal, social and physical education goal of using a simple process when making a choice. Key words: decision, choice, option, consequence, short-term, long-term, impulse, reason, review.

Stopping before acting uses inhibitory control. This is one of the core executive functions, and it is still growing through childhood (Diamond, 2013). Programmes such as Stop Think Do teach a short routine. Stop and calm down. Think of options and what each would lead to. Then do the one you chose, and check how it went. Practise it on small, everyday problems, so it is easier to use when feelings run high.

Common mistakes: acting on the first idea; thinking there is only one option; thinking only about now, not later; thinking only about yourself; giving a reason that is not about what will happen, such as it was my first idea; and giving up, or doing the same thing again, when a choice does not work.

In the lab your child stops a first idea before it happens and finds three more options. They match four options to what is likely to happen when a friend cheats. They slide from now to next week to compare two choices. They pick a choice and a reason, and find two good next tries when a choice fails.

practice.prompt: What is the first step when something goes wrong?
practice.hint: Before you think of options, what gives you time?
practice.explain: Stopping first gives you time to think. A first idea comes fast and is often not the best one.

practice.prompt: You think of {n} options for a problem. Then you think of 1 more. How many options do you have now?
practice.hint: Count on 1 from the options you had.
practice.explain: {n} and 1 more is {=n+1} options. More options give you more to compare.

choices: What happens because of a choice
practice.hint: Think: I chose this, so then that happened.
practice.explain: A consequence is what happens because of a choice. It can be good or bad, now or later.

practice.prompt: You have {n} sweets. You eat 2 now and save the rest for later. How many do you save?
practice.hint: Take the 2 you eat away from all your sweets.
practice.explain: {n} take away 2 is {=n-2}, so you save {=n-2} sweets. Thinking about later means some are still left tomorrow.

practice.prompt: Which reason shows you thought about what will happen?
choices: I will tidy up first, so I can find my toys later
practice.hint: A good reason says what will happen because of the choice.
practice.explain: Finding your toys later is a consequence, so that reason shows you thought ahead. The others do not say what will happen.

pool.prompt: Your friend takes your pencil without asking. What is the best first step?
pool.hint: The first step comes before you do anything at all.
pool.explain: Stop and breathe first. Then you can think of options, like asking for it back.

pool.prompt: Why should you think of more than one option?
choices: So you can compare them and pick the best
You should not, the first is best
pool.hint: With only one option, can you really choose?
pool.explain: With two or more options you can compare what each would do and pick the best one.

pool.prompt: Eating all your sweets now feels great. What might happen later?
choices: A tummy ache, and none left
pool.hint: Think about tomorrow, not just right now.
pool.explain: A choice can feel good now and bad later. Eating them all could mean a tummy ache and no sweets tomorrow.

pool.prompt: When you think about consequences, whose feelings count?
pool.hint: Who else might a choice affect?
pool.explain: A choice can affect other people as well as you, so think about everyone it touches.

pool.prompt: You think of {n} options. 2 of them could hurt someone. How many options are left to choose from?
pool.hint: Take away the options that could hurt someone.
pool.explain: {n} take away 2 is {=n-2} options left. Thinking about consequences helps you drop the bad ones.

pool.prompt: Your choice did not work. What should you do?
choices: Go back and try another option
Do the same thing again, louder
pool.hint: You thought of more than one option. Where are the others?
pool.explain: If one option fails, go back to your list and try the next one.

pool.prompt: {n} children want the one swing. Which option is most likely to work for everyone?
pool.hint: Which option gives all {n} children a go and keeps everyone safe?
pool.explain: Taking turns gives all {n} children a go. Racing or pushing leaves some out or gets someone hurt.

pool.prompt: Which one is a long-term consequence?
choices: Getting better at reading by next year
Laughing at a joke right now
pool.hint: Long-term means a long time after the choice.
pool.explain: Getting better by next year happens a long time later, so it is long-term. The others happen right now.

pool.prompt: A friend cheated and asks you to keep it a secret. Which option gives them a chance to own up?
pool.hint: Which option lets your friend fix it themselves?
pool.explain: Talking first gives your friend a chance to own up. Telling everyone shames them, and pretending lets the cheating go on.
